newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-Italy/EMU worries flare after Belgian comment.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy/EMU worries flare after Belgian comment.

text.p: Worries that Italy might be left out of Europe's single currency at the start hurt the lira and lira bonds on Tuesday after a Belgian central banker was quoted as saying Italy was in no shape to join the union.

Central bank governor Alfons Verplaetse denied a newspaper report which quoted him as saying economic and monetary union (EMU) should start without Italy since Rome would not be able to meet the economic entry criteria on government budget deficits.
But the lira failed to shake off market concern that Italy would be left out of the first wave of EMU due to start in 1999.
Verplaetse told Reuters he made no comments about the timing of Italy's membership of EMU in a speech on Monday.
"I did not say that," he said when asked about the report in the Belgian daily De Financieel Economische Tijd.

Verplaetse said he used the speech to talk about credible convergence plans, a strict adherence to the entry criteria and the sustainable character of measures which governments must take to meet the criteria. "But I made no allusion to Italy."

"What I did say was that I favour an unimpaired adherence to the criteria, no toughening and no relaxing. I said that I hope as many countries as possible will join from the start and by 2001 all of them (EU members) will be in (EMU)."
"Large changes in government deficits in a year's time... I have questions about that," he said.

The paper had quoted Verplaetse as saying: "I would not mind seeing countries with a government deficit of seven percent (of gross domestic product) lowering their deficit to three percent in a year's time and in a durable way. In my view that is not possible."

The paper concluded Verplaetse was speaking about Italy. It said Italy had a budget deficit/gross domestic product ratio of about seven percent in 1996 and aimed to cut the ratio to three percent in 1997 to be able to join EMU from the start.
The Maastricht Treaty sets a three percent deficit target for EU members to join EMU. Other criteria concern debt levels, and currency, interest rate and inflation stability.
Verplaetse told Reuters: "Three percent is sacred for Belgium...it is not up to me to have an opinion on Italy."

The paper said Verplaetse had doubts about an Italian plan to set a one-off tax to cut the deficit. "To raise taxes and promise that you partly pay them back next year...personally I feel a bit uneasy about that," it quoted him as saying.

Analysts have criticised the plan for being at odds with measures to achieve durable budget convergence between EU members, as outlined in the Maastricht Treaty. An EU ruling on various budgetary practices governments have used to bring deficits down to three percent of GDP is due later this week.

Political leaders will choose the first nations to adopt the new currency early in 1998. It is largely expected a core group of Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg and Ireland will definitely join EMU.
Traders and analysts said a combination of the Verplaetse comments and remarks from Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi late Monday hurt the currency and bond markets.
Prodi had said Germany was less committed to EMU than Italy.
At 1145 GMT the lira was at 989.57 per mark, down from 985.55 earlier and 987.25 late on Monday. Italian government bonds fell from opening levels but were off their lows by mid-session.
"The market is sensing a delay for Italy is in the offing," said Lee Ferridge, currency strategist at Commerzbank in London.
